newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM against NATO growth, seeks budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM against NATO growth, seeks budget deal.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, heading for a meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), criticised NATO's expansion plans on Sunday and asked parliament to approve Russia's 1997 budget.
Chernomyrdin told reporters Russia would not ease up on its tough opposition to NATO expansion at the Lisbon meeting of the 55-member OSCE.

"We are catagorically against the expansion of NATO to the east," Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying as he left Moscow. "Russia has its position and will stand by it at the OSCE meeting."
Russia has vigorously opposed NATO plans to take in some of Moscow's former East Bloc allies, but has also recognised that it can do little to halt the process.

Chernomyrdin said he accepted Russia had no right of veto on NATO expansion but said other states should take Moscow's views into account. He said the OSCE should become the basis for European security structures and such issues should not be tackled without Russia.
Itar-Tass news agency said Chernomyrdin also met parliamentary leaders on Sunday and urged them to approve the 1997 budget.

He said he would attend the State Duma lower house of parliament on December 6 to outline the government's medium-term economic programme and talk about the budget, which the Duma has already rejected once.
"Delaying approval of the state budget for next year could have political consequences," Chernomyrdin said.
Deputies in the communist-dominated lower house of parliament have said the spending plans do not meet the needs of Russians who have lost out under painful economic reforms.
Chernomyrdin said deputies had dragged their heels on approving legislation on taxation which formed a crucial part of the overall spending plans.

The prime minister was not in parliament on Friday when deputies criticised President Boris Yeltsin's peace moves in breakaway Chechnya, complaining that they would lead to the disintegration of the Russian Federation.
But deputies stopped short of implementing threats to start impeachment proceedings against Yeltsin and shelved plans to call for a vote of no-confidence in Chernomydin's government.

Yeltsin, bowing to the inevitable after Russian forces were humiliated by determined Chechen independence fighters, has said all Russian troops will leave the Caucasus region before the local authorities there hold elections next month.

One trainload of troops and equipment left the main Russian base at Khankala on Saturday and more soldiers will follow them out, rebasing in the southern Russian town of Budennovsk, scene of a bloody raid by guerrilla fighters in June last year.
Yeltsin sent troops into Chechnya in December 1994 to quell the region's bid for independence.
The president is recovering from a quintuple heart bypass operation in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow and his doctor said on Saturday that he was doing well.
"The state of Boris Yeltsin's health is normal, everything is stable. There is no need to wish for better," Itar-Tass news agency quoted heart surgeon Renat Akchurin as saying.
Yeltsin, dogged by ill health, has spent very little time in the Kremlin since he was re-elected for a second term on July 3.
